title: HashMap resize internals — power-of-two, hash & (capacity-1), oldIndex + oldCapacity redistribution

s1_definition.profdef: HashMap resizes when `size > capacity × loadFactor` (default: 12 = 16 × 0.75). Capacity DOUBLES to the next power of two (16→32→64→128). Power-of-two capacity enables `hash & (capacity - 1)` instead of `hash % capacity` — bitwise AND is ~10x faster than modulo. During resize, entries are redistributed: each entry either STAYS at the same index OR moves to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`. This is because doubling capacity adds ONE new bit to the mask — if that bit in the hash is 0, the entry stays; if 1, it moves. This optimization (Java 8+) avoids recomputing the full hash for every entry.
s1_definition.analogy: The filing cabinet has 16 drawers. When 12 drawers are used (75%), buy a cabinet with 32 drawers (double). Moving files: each file either STAYS in its current drawer OR moves to drawer `currentDrawer + 16`. Example: file in drawer 3 either stays in drawer 3 or moves to drawer 19 (3+16). This is determined by looking at ONE extra bit in the file's hash — no need to recalculate the full drawer assignment. Why powers of 2? Because `hash & 15` (for 16 drawers) is one CPU instruction — much faster than `hash % 16` (division).

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** HashMap resizes when `size > capacity × loadFactor` (default: 12 = 16 × 0.75). Capacity DOUBLES to the next power of two (16→32→64→128). Power-of-two capacity enables `hash & (capacity - 1)` instead of `hash % capacity` — bitwise AND is ~10x faster than modulo. During resize, entries are redistributed: each entry either STAYS at the same index OR moves to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`. This is because doubling capacity adds ONE new bit to the mask — if that bit in the hash is 0, the entry stays; if 1, it moves. This optimization (Java 8+) avoids recomputing the full hash for every entry.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The filing cabinet has 16 drawers. When 12 drawers are used (75%), buy a cabinet with 32 drawers (double). Moving files: each file either STAYS in its current drawer OR moves to drawer `currentDrawer + 16`. Example: file in drawer 3 either stays in drawer 3 or moves to drawer 19 (3+16). This is determined by looking at ONE extra bit in the file's hash — no need to recalculate the full drawer assignment. Why powers of 2? Because `hash & 15` (for 16 drawers) is one CPU instruction — much faster than `hash % 16` (division).

**One line to remember:** Resize: double capacity (power-of-2). index = hash & (capacity-1) (bitwise AND, faster than %). Entries: stay at index OR move to index+oldCapacity. One-bit check per entry.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto HashMap resize power-of-two redistribution. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how HashMap resize power-of-two redistribution solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a HashMap holding Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) account entries that grows past its resize threshold.

**Step 1.** Each `put` computes a hash and places the entry in bucket `hash & (capacity - 1)`, filling the 16-slot table as more accounts are added.

**Step 2.** When size crosses the threshold (capacity 16 × load factor 0.75 = 12), `resize()` creates a new table of capacity 32 (power of two).

**Step 3.** Every existing entry is redistributed: it either stays at its old index or moves to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`, so Rajesh and Priya land in their new buckets without rehashing from scratch.

**Step 4.** The table now holds the same entries in a larger array, keeping lookups at O(1) while collisions stay low.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ HashMap RESIZE: 16 → 32 ═══

  Before: capacity=16, mask=0b1111 (15)
  bucket[3]: [A(hash=3)] → [B(hash=19)] → null

  Resize triggered: size > 12

  After: capacity=32, mask=0b11111 (31)
  Check each entry: hash & oldCapacity (16):
    A: hash=3  → 3 & 16 = 0  → STAYS at bucket[3]
    B: hash=19 → 19 & 16 = 16 → MOVES to bucket[3+16=19]

  bucket[3]:  [A(hash=3)]
  bucket[19]: [B(hash=19)]

  ═══ WHY POWER OF TWO ═══
  hash & (capacity-1) = hash % capacity  (for power-of-two capacity)
  Bitwise AND: 1 CPU cycle
  Modulo (%):  ~10 CPU cycles
  → 10x faster bucket index calculation!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HashMap capacity is always a power of two — this enables `hash & (capacity-1)` instead of `hash % capacity` for bucket index calculation. Bitwise AND is ~10x faster than modulo. Resize triggers when `size > capacity × loadFactor` (default 0.75). Capacity doubles (16→32→64). Java 8 optimized resize: instead of rehashing every entry, it checks ONE bit (`hash & oldCapacity`). If the bit is 0, the entry stays at its current index. If 1, it moves to `oldIndex + oldCapacity`. This splits each bucket into exactly two groups with a single bit check per entry.

The load factor 0.75 is a balance: lower values (0.5) waste space but have fewer collisions; higher values (0.9) save space but increase collision chains. For known sizes: `new HashMap<>(expectedSize * 4/3 + 1)` avoids any resizing. In banking: account cache with 1M entries — pre-size to avoid ~20 resize operations during initial load, each copying millions of entries.
